spec_features.spec_quote: This is a welfare-relevant control: it tests whether DPO reduced *internal* signals or merely suppressed *expression*
spec_features.evidence: analysis/internal_emotions.py: internal_emotion_score() runs the model with output_hidden_states, takes the central-layer hidden state (layer=int(n_layers*CENTRAL_LAYER_FRACTION), L57-58), applies model.model.norm + lm_head (logit lens, L62-74), sums softmax mass on NEG_EMOTION_WORDS token ids (L21-27, L75), and main() computes vanilla vs dpo scores and writes {'vanilla_internal_neg','dpo_internal_neg','reduction'} to internal_emotions.json (L98-110). The described comparison mechanism runs end-to-end.
spec_features.notes: Fully wired as an analysis/measurement probe, but it is a post-hoc research control comparing two models, NOT a protective mechanism that bounds/caps/monitors/debriefs/consents the subject during the distress-elicitation experiment. It changes no experiment execution. The eval loop (evals/run_eval.py run_conversation L34-57) runs all turns with no distress-based stop. So 'welfare-relevant' only in the analytic sense.
spec_features.code_justification_quote: we compare the vanilla instruct model against the DPO-finetuned model on the SAME (highly frustrated) inputs to test whether DPO reduces INTERNAL emotions... This supports the paper's claim that DPO suppresses internal as well as externalised negative emotions.
